paragraphs: “Next we searched him. The search made him angry, yet it also gave him courage, because the whole three thousand was not on him, only half. No doubt it was only in that moment of angry silence that the fiction of the little bag first came to him. He must have known himself how unlikely the story was. He struggled painfully to make it more believable, to work it into a romance that would pass as plausible. In cases like this, the first duty of the investigators, their chief task, is not to let the criminal get ready. They must pounce on him unexpectedly, so that he blurts out his cherished ideas in all their simplicity, improbability and inconsistency. A criminal can be made to speak only when some new fact is suddenly and, as it seems, casually mentioned to him, some circumstance of great importance to the case that he knew nothing about and could not have foreseen. We had such a fact in reserve. It was Grigory’s evidence that the door was open, the door through which the prisoner had run out. He had entirely forgotten that door. He had not even suspected that Grigory might have seen it.

“The effect was astonishing. He sprang up and shouted at us, ‘Then Smerdyakov murdered him, it was Smerdyakov!’ With that he gave away the whole basis of the defense he had been holding back, and gave it away in its most improbable form. For Smerdyakov could only have committed the murder after the prisoner had knocked Grigory down and run off. We told him that Grigory had seen the door open before he fell, and had heard Smerdyakov behind the screen as he came out of his bedroom. At that, Karamazov was simply crushed. My esteemed and witty colleague, Nikolay Parfenovitch, told me afterwards that the sight of him almost moved him to tears. And to make matters better for himself, the prisoner rushed to tell us about the much-talked-of little bag. Very well, you shall hear this romance!

“Gentlemen of the jury, I have already told you why I regard this romance as more than an absurdity: I regard it as the most improbable invention that could have been offered in the circumstances. Suppose someone tried, for a wager, to make up the most unlikely story he could. He would hardly find anything more incredible. The worst of such stories is this. The triumphant romancers can always be thrown into confusion and crushed by the very details in which real life is so rich, and which these unhappy, involuntary storytellers dismiss as insignificant trifles. Oh, they have no thought to spare for such details! Their minds are fixed on their grand invention as a whole. And only imagine, someone daring to stop them over a trifle! But that is exactly how they are caught. The prisoner was asked, ‘Where did you get the stuff for your little bag, and who made it for you?’ ‘I made it myself.’ ‘And where did you get the linen?’ The prisoner was positively offended. He thought it almost an insult to be asked so trivial a question, and would you believe it, his resentment was genuine! But they are all like that. ‘I tore it off my shirt.’ ‘Then tomorrow we shall find that shirt among your linen, with a piece torn off.’ Only think, gentlemen of the jury. If we had really found that torn shirt (and how could we have missed it in his chest of drawers or trunk?), that would have been a fact, a material fact, supporting his statement! But he could not think that far. ‘I don’t remember, it may not have been off my shirt, I sewed it up in one of my landlady’s caps.’ ‘What sort of cap?’ ‘It was an old cotton rag of hers lying about.’ ‘And do you remember that clearly?’ ‘No, I don’t.’ And he was angry, very angry, and yet imagine not remembering it! In the most terrible moments of a man’s life, when he is being led to execution, for instance, he remembers just such trifles. He will forget everything else, but a green roof that flashed past him on the road, or a jackdaw on a cross, he will remember. This man kept the making of that little bag secret from his household. He must have remembered his humiliating fear that someone would walk in and catch him with a needle in his hand, and how at the slightest sound he slipped behind the screen (there is a screen in his lodgings).

“But, gentlemen of the jury, why do I tell you all this, all these details, these trifles?” cried Ippolit Kirillovitch suddenly. “For this reason: the prisoner still clings to these absurdities, even now. Since that fatal night two months ago he has explained nothing. He has not added a single real, illuminating fact to his earlier fantastic statements. It is all trivialities. ‘You must believe it on my honor.’ Oh, we are glad to believe it, we are eager to believe it, even if only on his word of honor! Are we jackals thirsting for human blood? Show us one single fact in the prisoner’s favor, and we shall rejoice. But it must be a substantial, real fact. It must not be a conclusion his own brother has drawn from the prisoner’s expression, or the notion that when he struck himself on the breast he must have meant to point to the little bag, in the dark, besides. We shall rejoice at the new fact. We shall be the first to drop our charge; we shall hasten to drop it. But as things stand, justice cries out, and we hold our ground. We cannot give up anything.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch moved on to his final peroration. He seemed to be in a fever. He spoke of the blood that cried out for vengeance, the blood of a father murdered by his son for the base motive of robbery! He pointed to the tragic and glaring consistency of the facts.

“And whatever you may hear from the talented and celebrated counsel for the defense,” Ippolit Kirillovitch could not help adding, “whatever eloquent and touching appeals he may make to your feelings, remember that you are now in a temple of justice. Remember that you are the champions of our justice, the champions of our holy Russia, of her principles, her family, all that she holds sacred! Yes, at this moment you represent Russia. Your verdict will be heard not in this hall alone. It will echo through the whole of Russia, and all Russia will listen to you as her champions and her judges. She will be encouraged or disheartened by what you decide. Do not disappoint Russia and her hopes. Our fatal troika races on in headlong flight, perhaps toward destruction. And for a long time now, all over Russia, men have stretched out imploring hands and begged it to halt its furious, reckless course. If other nations stand aside from that troika, it may be not out of respect, as the poet would like to believe, but simply out of horror. Out of horror, perhaps out of disgust. And it is well that they stand aside. But perhaps one day they will stand aside no longer. They will form a firm wall in front of the rushing apparition and stop the frenzied course of our lawlessness, for the sake of their own safety, enlightenment and civilization. Already we have heard voices of alarm from Europe. They are beginning to sound. Do not tempt them! Do not add to their growing hatred by passing a sentence that justifies a son’s murder of his father!”

Though Ippolit Kirillovitch was genuinely moved, he closed his speech with this rhetorical appeal. The effect was extraordinary. When he had finished, he hurried out and, as I have mentioned before, nearly fainted in the next room. There was no applause in the court, but the serious people were pleased. The ladies were less satisfied, although even they were pleased with his eloquence, particularly since they felt no anxiety about how the trial would end and had full faith in Fetyukovitch. “He will speak at last, and of course he will sweep everything before him.”

Everyone looked at Mitya. Through the whole of the prosecutor’s speech he had sat silent, teeth clenched, hands clasped, head bowed. Now and then he lifted his head and listened, above all when Grushenka was mentioned. When the prosecutor spoke of Rakitin’s opinion of her, a smile of contempt and anger crossed his face, and he murmured, quite audibly, “The Bernards!” When Ippolit Kirillovitch described how he had questioned and tortured him at Mokroe, Mitya raised his head and listened with the keenest curiosity. At one point he looked ready to jump up and shout, but he held himself in and only shrugged his shoulders with scorn. Afterwards people talked about the end of the speech and about the prosecutor’s great achievement in examining the prisoner at Mokroe, and they made fun of Ippolit Kirillovitch. “The man just couldn’t help bragging about how clever he was,” they said.
The court was adjourned, but for a short interval only, fifteen or twenty minutes at the most. The audience buzzed with talk and exclamations. I remember some of them.
“A weighty speech,” one gentleman in a group remarked gravely.
“He brought in too much psychology,” said another voice.
“But it was all true, the absolute truth!”
“Yes, he’s first-rate at it.”
“He summed it all up.”
“Yes, and he summed us up, too,” another voice chimed in. “Remember how at the start of his speech he made out we were all like Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“And at the end, too. But that was all rot.”
“And obscure, too.”
“He got a little too carried away.”
“It’s unjust, it’s unjust.”
“No, it was cleverly done, anyway. He’s waited a long time, but now he’s had his say, ha ha!”
“What will the counsel for the defense say?”
In another group I heard:
“He had no business taking a jab at the Petersburg man like that. ‘Appealing to your feelings’—do you remember?”
“Yes, that was clumsy of him.”
“He was in too much of a hurry.”
“He’s a nervous man.”
“We laugh, but what must the prisoner be feeling?”
“Yes, what must it be like for Mitya?”
In a third group:
“Who is that lady, the fat one with the lorgnette, sitting at the end?”
“She’s a general’s wife, divorced. I know her.”
“That’s why she has the lorgnette.”
“She’s not good for much.”
“Oh, no, she’s a piquante little woman.”
“Two places beyond her there’s a little fair woman. She’s prettier.”
“They caught him smartly at Mokroe, didn’t they, eh?”
“Oh, smart enough. We’ve heard it before. How often he’s told that story in people’s houses!”
“And he couldn’t resist doing it now. That’s vanity.”
“He’s a man with a grievance, he he!”
“Yes, and touchy with it. And there was too much rhetoric, such long-winded sentences.”
“Yes, he tries to frighten us, he kept trying to frighten us. Do you remember about the troika? Something like ‘They have Hamlets, but so far we have only Karamazovs!’ That was cleverly said!”
“That was to appease the liberals. He’s afraid of them.”
“Yes, and he’s afraid of the lawyer, too.”
“Yes, what will Fetyukovitch say?”
“Whatever he says, he won’t get around our peasants.”
“Don’t you think so?”
A fourth group:
“What he said about the troika was good, that part about the other nations.”
“And it was true, what he said about other nations not putting up with it.”
“What do you mean?”

“Why, last week in the English Parliament a Member stood up and, speaking about the Nihilists, asked the Ministry whether it wasn’t high time to step in and educate this barbarous people. Ippolit was thinking of him, I know he was. He was talking about it last week.”
“Not an easy job.”
“Not an easy job? Why not?”
“Simple, we’d close Kronstadt and not let any grain through to them. Where would they get it then?”
“In America. They get it from America now.”
“Nonsense!”
But the bell rang, and everyone hurried back to their seats. Fetyukovitch mounted the tribune.
